sections.title: *Heilakh*: Partial Admission or Full Denial? R. Chiya vs. Rav Sheshet
sections.gist: Continuing R. Chiya's ruling that one who admits fifty and says "here you are" must still swear on the rest. The section covers his proof from the garment Mishnah, Rav Sheshet's exemption, and whether a rabbinic oath needs a Torah model.

children.title: The Garment Mishnah: Each Holder's Half as "Here You Are"
children.gist: R. Chiya's support: each holder of the garment effectively has his half handed to him, and the Mishnah still has him swear.

bullets.text: In the Mishnah of two holding a garment, each grasps half. What each holds is clearly his, as if the other had said to him "here you are, I am giving it to you."
The Mishnah still has each one take an oath. So a defendant who denies part of a claim and says "here you are" about the rest must swear.

The lecturer notes that the garment case is really "witnesses on half": each side's evidence is his physical possession, and the two sides' evidence is exactly equal. That symmetry is why its oath cannot be a Torah-level partial admission, which is the opening Rav Sheshet will use.

children.title: Rav Sheshet: The Handed-Over Money Is Already the Lender's, So a Full Denial
children.gist: Rav Sheshet exempts one who says "here you are": what he admits is already in the lender's hands, and all that is left is a denial.

bullets.text: Rav Sheshet: one who says "here you are" about part of the claim and denies the rest is exempt from an oath.
His reason: the dinars he admits are as if the creditor already has them. He did not admit owing the other fifty, so there is no partial admission here.
In effect the remaining dispute is a *kofer ha'kol* over fifty, and a full denial carries no Torah oath.

children.title: The Garment Oath: *Takkanat Chakhamim*, but With or Without a Torah Model?
children.gist: Rav Sheshet answers the garment Mishnah by calling its oath rabbinic. R. Chiya agrees that it is rabbinic, but asks whether the Sages would enact an oath that has no counterpart in Torah law.

bullets.text: Challenge to Rav Sheshet: the garment Mishnah looks like the same case, and it requires an oath.
Rav Sheshet: that oath is a rabbinic ordinance for that case alone. In general, one who hands over what he admits is exempt.
The lecturer suggests the Sages enacted it to keep people from grabbing things and claiming them as their own.

R. Chiya grants that the oath is rabbinic. But if *heilakh* obligates an oath by Torah law, the Sages modeled their oath on it. If it is exempt by Torah law, would the Sages have instituted an oath with no Torah counterpart?

A deeper edge to the argument: if *heilakh* is exempt, Torah logic applied to the garment case (each half already "handed over") would yield no oath at all. The rabbinic oath would then run against Torah reasoning, not merely lack a model.

sections.title: The Unspecified Note: Is the Documented Minimum Like "Here You Are"?
sections.gist: A baraita about a note with no amount is used against each side in turn: R. Shimon ben Elazar against R. Chiya, and R. Akiva against Rav Sheshet. Both challenges are deflected, and admitting the note's two dinars turns out to be exempt for reasons of its own.

chart.caption: The baraita used against each side of the *heilakh* dispute
rows: Against R. Chiya (from R. Shimon ben Elazar)
Only admitting three obligates; admitting two, which is like *heilakh*, is exempt
Two also obligates; three is named only to answer R. Akiva
The deflection fails on the wording. Two is exempt, but because the note supports him or because of the lien on land
Against Rav Sheshet (from R. Akiva)
Only admitting three exempts; admitting two, which is like *heilakh*, obligates
Two is also exempt; three is named only to answer R. Shimon ben Elazar
The deflection holds, since otherwise the debtor could game the rule by saying three

children.title: Baraita: Five Claimed, Three Admitted: Partial Admission or Returning a Lost Item?
children.gist: A note records a loan of unspecified *sela'im* or dinars. R. Shimon ben Elazar requires an oath of one who admits three, and R. Akiva exempts him as one returning a lost item.

bullets.text: The Gemara brings a baraita to object to R. Chiya. A promissory note says "*sela'im*" or "dinars" with no number. The creditor says five *sela*, the debtor says three.
R. Shimon ben Elazar: since he admitted part of the claim, he takes an oath.
R. Akiva: the note's plural wording proves only two, the minimum plural. By admitting three he is like one returning a lost item (*meshiv aveidah*), and he is exempt.

The logic of *meshiv aveidah*: he could have said two and nothing could contradict him. Imposing an oath for volunteering more would discourage honest admissions. The lecturer leaves open whether this is a policy of the Sages or a *migo*-type argument.

children.title: Challenge to R. Chiya: R. Shimon ben Elazar Implies Admitting Two Is Exempt
children.gist: The inference that the note's two dinars are like "here you are" and exempt, a failed attempt to deflect it, and the Gemara's answer that two is exempt for other reasons.

children.title: The Inference: The Note's Two Dinars Are Like "Here You Are"
children.gist: R. Shimon ben Elazar obligates because the debtor said three, which implies that admitting two, already in the note, would be exempt.

bullets.text: R. Shimon ben Elazar obligates "since he admitted part", that is, because he said three. Had he admitted only two, he would be exempt.
An obligation already recorded in a note is like one about which the debtor says "here you are". So one who says "here you are" is exempt, against R. Chiya.
Before a word is said in court, the note already proves two, so the only live dispute is above that minimum.

children.title: Deflection Rejected: The Baraita Would Have Said "Even This One"
children.gist: Perhaps admitting two obligates too, and three is named only to answer R. Akiva; but then the baraita would have been worded "even this one swears."

bullets.text: Proposal: even admitting two obligates an oath. The dispute is set at three only to reject R. Akiva's view of the debtor as one returning a lost item.
Rejected: then R. Shimon ben Elazar should have said "even this one, who admits three, swears", not "since he admitted part of the claim, he swears."

children.title: Two Is Exempt, but Not as *Heilakh*: The Note's Support or the Land Lien
children.gist: Admitting two is exempt, yet "here you are" still obligates. The two dinars are exempt either because the note supports the debtor or because a note creates a lien on land.

bullets.text: Conclusion: admitting two is exempt, and still one who says "here you are" must swear. This case is different because the note supports him: it shows he owes two.
Alternatively: a promissory note creates a lien on the debtor's land (*shibud karka'ot*), and no oath is taken over the denial of a debt secured by land. Oaths apply only to money and movables.
A note works like two witnesses: its plural wording proves two with the force of testimony, so the debtor's "admission" of two adds nothing.

The lien reaches exactly what the note proves, two. Admitting two admits only a land-lien obligation. Admitting three adds one dinar of plain money outside the lien, and that is a genuine partial admission.

children.title: Challenge to Rav Sheshet: R. Akiva Implies Admitting Two Obligates
children.gist: Some read R. Akiva as obligating one who admits two, against Rav Sheshet. The Gemara deflects this and proves the deflection from the debtor's possible ploy, which brings the answers for R. Chiya back.

children.title: The Inference: Only Three Is Returning a Lost Item
children.gist: R. Akiva exempts because the debtor said three, which implies that admitting two, like "here you are", would obligate.

bullets.text: Some raise the challenge from the baraita's second half. R. Akiva exempts because the debtor said three, so had he said two he would have to swear.
The note's two dinars are like "here you are", so one who says "here you are" must swear, against Rav Sheshet.

children.title: Deflection: Three Is Named Only to Answer R. Shimon ben Elazar
children.gist: R. Akiva also exempts one who admits two. He speaks of three only to reject R. Shimon ben Elazar's partial-admission view.

bullets.text: The Gemara answers that admitting two is exempt for R. Akiva too. The dispute is set at three to reject R. Shimon ben Elazar, who treats that debtor as one who admits part of the claim.
R. Akiva's point is that admitting three makes the debtor like one returning a lost item, and so exempt.

children.title: Proof: Otherwise the Debtor Would Say Three to Escape the Oath
children.gist: If admitting two obligated an oath, R. Akiva's exemption for three would invite a ploy, so admitting two must be exempt.

bullets.text: The Gemara supports this reading. If admitting two obligated an oath, how could R. Akiva exempt one who admits three?
The debtor might be scheming: "If I say two, I must swear. I'll say three, count as returning a lost item, and be exempt." So even admitting two must be exempt.
The underlying assumption is that the Sages do not frame a rule that an informed litigant could easily game.

children.title: Back to R. Chiya: The Note's Support or the Land Lien Again
children.gist: Exempting one who admits two now seems to refute R. Chiya, and the same two answers apply: the note supports him, or the note is a lien on land.

bullets.text: Challenge: if one who admits two is exempt, this contradicts R. Chiya, who obligates one who says "here you are."
Answer: that case is different because the note supports him. Alternatively, the note creates a lien on land, and no oath is taken over the denial of a debt secured by land.

returns_to.note: The same two answers given earlier for R. Shimon ben Elazar's version

children.continues: The *heilakh* dispute continues: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Nachman, challenges Rav Sheshet from the Mishnah in Shevuot on a claim of vessels and land.

key_terms.sense: handing over the admitted part of a claim on the spot
key_terms.definition: A defendant who says "here you are" and immediately hands over the part of the claim he admits. The question is whether he still counts as admitting part of the claim.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Chiya holds that one who says heilakh must still swear on the rest. Rav Sheshet exempts him, since the money handed over counts as the lender's already.

key_terms.sense: admitting part of a monetary claim
key_terms.definition: A defendant who admits part of a monetary claim and denies the rest. By Torah law he must take an oath on the part he denies.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks whether handing over the admitted part, or admitting only what a note already proves, still counts as a partial admission.

key_terms.definition: A defendant who denies the whole claim against him. Without other evidence, Torah law imposes no oath on him.
key_terms.on_this_daf: For Rav Sheshet, once the admitted money is handed over, the defendant is a kofer ha'kol on what remains.

key_terms.definition: A law instituted by the Sages rather than derived from the Torah, often modeled on a Torah law.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Both sides call the garment Mishnah's oath a rabbinic ordinance. R. Chiya argues that it must have a Torah model, the oath of heilakh.

key_terms.sense: one who volunteers what could not be proven against him
key_terms.definition: One who returns a lost item he could have kept. By extension, a litigant who admits more than could be proven against him is treated like him and exempt from an oath.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Akiva treats a debtor who admits three, when the note proves only two, as returning a lost item, and exempts him.

key_terms.sense: a debt secured by a lien on land
key_terms.definition: The lien that a written loan document creates on the debtor's real estate. Claims about land, including debts secured by it, are not subject to the oath of partial admission.
key_terms.on_this_daf: One reason a debtor who admits only the note's two dinars takes no oath: that obligation is secured by a lien on land.

judgment_calls: The baraita of the unspecified note (4a.19–4b.10) could be nested under the heilakh dispute, since both challenges test R. Chiya and Rav Sheshet. Made it a separate top-level section because it is a self-contained source with its own case and machinery, tested against each side in turn.

The garment Mishnah's proof (4a.15) could be merged into the heilakh parent's bullets. Kept it as a child so that R. Chiya's proof, Rav Sheshet's view and the debate over the rabbinic oath read as three steps.
4b.10 repeats the two answers of 4b.5–4b.6. Kept it where it falls, under the challenge to Rav Sheshet, with a returns_to link, rather than merging it with the earlier section.

The two challenges from the baraita could be arranged as one section each for R. Shimon ben Elazar and R. Akiva, with the challenges beneath them. Followed the Gemara's order of challenge, deflection and answer instead.
coverage_notes: The shiur material on 4a.1–4a.14 (the one-witness and gilgul inferences, the common-denominator argument, the concern that the defendant is a proven liar, conspiring witnesses, why the garment Mishnah doesn't match R. Chiya's two-witness ruling, and R. Chiya's statement of the heilakh ruling) is outside this outline's scope.

The Gemara from 4b.11 on (Mar Zutra's challenge from the Mishnah in Shevuot, the binding of a land claim to an oath, and the Mishnah in Kiddushin) is outside this outline's scope; the shiur doesn't reach it either.
The essay calls the tanna 'Rabban Shimon ben Elazar'; the text has Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. Followed the text.

The essay describes the note as recording dinars, with claims of five and three dinars. The text says the note has an unspecified number of sela'im or dinars, the creditor claims five sela, and the debtor says three; R. Akiva speaks of two dinars as the minimum plural. Followed the text.

The essay presents the baraita as an analysis of the two positions. The text brings it first as an objection to R. Chiya (4a.19) and then, 'there are those who', as an objection to Rav Sheshet (4b.7). Followed the text's structure.

The essay lists three convergent grounds for exempting one who admits two, one of them heilakh. The text gives two alternative answers (the note supports him; a lien on land), and at 4b.5 explicitly keeps heilakh as obligating. Followed the text.
The essay's step at 4b.3–4b.4 (the deflection rejected on the wording 'even this one') is barely discussed in the shiur; outlined from the text.

The essay says R. Chiya 'emerges with his original position intact' after the rabbinic-oath argument. The text records no reply from Rav Sheshet and no ruling, so the outline doesn't state a resolution.
